Virtuous
vẽr´tū-us
adj. (of moral strength and worth; rendering Hebrew chayil)
From Latin virtus, manliness, strength, excellence. The Hebrew word behind it, chayil, is a military term for force and ability.

Biblical Definition

Virtuous in Scripture means strong in moral worth, and the Hebrew is bracing: chayil is the word for an army, for valour, for substance. “Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies” (Pro 31:10) is therefore not a portrait of decorative gentility but of formidable capability under God. Boaz uses it of Ruth — “all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman” (Rut 3:11) — and Proverbs makes the domestic consequence plain: “A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband” (Pro 12:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines virtuous as morally good, acting in conformity to the moral law; and as being efficacious by inherent qualities.

expand to see more

VIRTUOUS, a. Morally good; acting in conformity to the moral law; practising the moral duties, and abstaining from vice.

2. Being in conformity to the moral or divine law; as a virtuous action.

3. Chaste; applied to women.

4. Efficacious by inherent qualities; as virtuous herbs.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:10 — "Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies."

Rut 3:11 — "And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman."

Pro 12:4 — "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones."

Pro 31:29 — "Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all."

Modern Corruption

Proverbs 31 is read either as an impossible standard that shames women or as a decorative ideal that patronizes them — both miss that chayil is the vocabulary of strength.

expand to see more

The word choice governs the whole chapter. Chayil describes armies, wealth, and valour; when it is applied to a woman the picture that follows matches — she buys a field, plants a vineyard, trades profitably, arms herself with strength, opens her hand to the poor, and laughs at the time to come. This is not a wife decorating a household but a woman deploying formidable competence within it. Reading the chapter as a checklist of chores misses the genre; it is a poem in praise of strength.

Ruth is the flesh on the definition, and the detail matters: she was a Moabitess, a widow, and destitute, gleaning behind reapers for survival. What made the whole city call her a woman of chayil was not her circumstances but her covenant loyalty to Naomi and her willingness to work. Virtue in Scripture is available to the poor, which is precisely what a decorative reading of Proverbs 31 makes impossible.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chayil (H2428), strength, force, ability, an army; used of Ruth, of the Proverbs 31 woman, and of mighty men of valour.

expand to see more

Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, valour, substance; Proverbs 31:10, Ruth 3:11, and the men of valour throughout Judges and Samuel.

Greek arete (G703) — virtue, moral excellence; 2 Peter 1:5, add to your faith virtue.

Hebrew ishshah chayil — woman of strength; the phrase Boaz applies to Ruth.

Usage

"“Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies” — strength, not decoration."

"“Thou art a virtuous woman” — said of a destitute foreign widow."

"“A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband” — the household consequence."
